title: Contingent Assets and Contingent Liabilities
outcomes: Define contingent assets and contingent liabilities in your own words and recognise them in practical situations.
State how each is treated — recognised, disclosed in notes, mentioned in the Board's report, or ignored.
Distinguish contingent liabilities from liabilities and from provisions, applying the recognition tests.
Account for a contingent liability that later becomes a provision.

meta.exam_tip: Remember the ladder: virtually certain → recognise asset; probable outflow → provision; possible → disclose; remote → nothing. Most questions are a list of situations to sort with this ladder.

concepts.title: Contingent asset
body: A contingent asset is a possible asset, arising out of past events, whose existence can be confirmed only when one or more uncertain future events, not fully under the enterprise's control, happen or fail to happen. It usually comes from unplanned or unexpected events that give a possibility of inflow of economic benefits — for example, a claim the enterprise is pursuing in court with an uncertain result.

Treatment: a contingent asset is not recognised in the accounts — recognising it could mean recording income that may never be realised (prudence and the accounting standards). It need not be disclosed in the financial statements; it is commonly mentioned in the approving authority's report (the Board of Directors' report for a company) if an inflow is probable.

Contingent assets are reviewed continually. When the inflow becomes virtually certain, it is no longer contingent: both the asset and the income it brings are booked in the period when that change takes place.
concepts.analogy: A lottery ticket you have bought: you may win, but you do not add the prize to your bank balance until the result is declared and the money is certain.
concepts.work: Clients often want a pending insurance or legal claim shown as income. The CA must hold back until it is virtually certain — for instance, the insurer has admitted the claim in writing.

concepts.title: Contingent liability
body: A contingent liability is (a) a possible obligation, arising out of past events, whose existence can be confirmed only when uncertain future events, not fully under the enterprise's control, happen or fail to happen; or (b) a present obligation arising from past events that is not recognised because an outflow of resources is not probable, or because the amount cannot be estimated reliably.

Treatment: not recognised in the balance sheet, but disclosed in the notes to accounts — unless the possibility of an outflow is remote, in which case nothing is disclosed. Contingent liabilities are reassessed continually; if an outflow becomes probable, a provision is recognised in the period in which the probability changes (except in the extremely rare case where no reliable estimate can be made).
Common examples: claims made against the enterprise that it has not accepted as debts, guarantees it has given for third parties, liability on bills discounted, and statutory dues under dispute.
concepts.analogy: Standing guarantor for a friend's loan: you owe nothing today, but you will have to pay if your friend defaults. You should tell anyone assessing your finances about it.
concepts.work: The "contingent liabilities" note is one of the first things a banker or analyst reads in an annual report — a large guarantee or tax dispute can change the credit decision.

concepts.title: Liability versus contingent liability
body: A liability is a present financial obligation arising from past events, whose settlement will cause an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits. It is recognised in the balance sheet.

A contingent liability lacks one of these: either the outflow is not probable, or the amount cannot be measured reliably (or the obligation is only possible). It is disclosed in notes, not recognised. The line between the two often depends on management's judgement.

blocks.title: Liability vs contingent liability

concepts.analogy: A bill you have received is a liability. A bill that may arrive if a dispute goes against you is a contingent liability.
concepts.work: Auditors send confirmation letters to the client's lawyers to understand pending cases and judge whether they are liabilities, provisions or merely contingent.

concepts.title: Provision versus contingent liability
body: Provision means an amount written off or retained to provide for depreciation, renewal or fall in value of assets, or retained to provide for a known liability whose amount cannot be determined with substantial accuracy.

A provision is recognised when (a) there is a present obligation from past events, (b) an outflow of resources is probable, and (c) a reliable estimate of the amount can be made. If any test fails, there is no provision — the item is disclosed as a contingent liability (unless remote).

Example: an excise penalty under appeal. If management thinks it will probably have to pay, it recognises a provision; if it expects the appeal to succeed and payment is less likely, it discloses a contingent liability.

blocks.title: Provision vs contingent liability

concepts.analogy: An umbrella you carry because rain is forecast (provision) versus a note in your diary that it might rain later in the week (contingent liability).
concepts.work: Warranty provisions, provisions for pending litigation and for doubtful debts are all estimates that auditors test. Over- or under-providing directly changes profit.

illustrations.title: Year-end review of claims, guarantees and disputes
illustrations.q: Orion Ltd is finalising accounts for the year ending 31 March 2027. (a) A customer has sued it for ₹12,00,000; its lawyers think a loss is probable and estimate it at ₹9,00,000. (b) A GST demand of ₹6,00,000 is under appeal and the company expects to win. (c) It has guaranteed a group company's bank loan of ₹25,00,000; the borrower is paying regularly. (d) Bills receivable of ₹4,00,000 discounted with the bank are not yet due. (e) It has a claim of ₹8,00,000 against a supplier; the outcome is uncertain but an inflow is probable. (f) An insurer has admitted a claim of ₹3,00,000 in writing, payable next month. (g) An ex-employee's claim of ₹50,000 is described by lawyers as baseless. State the treatment of each item, give the journal entries required and the effect on profit.

jobs.title: Reading the lawyer's confirmation letter
jobs.role: Audit senior on a company audit
jobs.situation: The company's legal counsel lists three cases: a customer claim of ₹40 lakh ("loss probable, likely settlement ₹25 lakh"), a labour dispute of ₹8 lakh ("unlikely to succeed"), and a trademark suit filed by the company for ₹60 lakh ("strong case").
steps: Customer claim: present obligation, probable outflow, reliable estimate → check that a provision of about ₹25 lakh is recognised.
Labour dispute: outflow not probable → check that it is disclosed as a contingent liability (not provided).
Trademark suit by the company: a contingent asset — must not be recognised as income; it may be mentioned in the Board's report if an inflow is probable.
Document the lawyer's opinion and management's assessment in the working papers.
jobs.takeaway: Probability decides everything: probable outflow → provision; possible → disclose; remote → ignore; and gains wait until virtually certain.
jobs.think: If the company's trademark suit were decided in its favour after the year end and the defendant paid in full, would the asset be recognised?
jobs.answer: Once the inflow is virtually certain, the asset and income are recognised in the period in which that change occurs — not by pretending it was certain earlier.

jobs.title: Explaining a guarantee to a promoter
jobs.situation: The promoter has made the company guarantee a ₹2 crore loan of his cousin's firm and asks why it must appear in the accounts when "nothing has been paid".
steps: Explain that a guarantee is a possible obligation depending on a future default — a contingent liability.
It is not recognised as a liability, but it must be disclosed in the notes so that lenders and shareholders know the risk.
If the cousin's firm starts defaulting and payment becomes probable, a provision will be needed.
jobs.takeaway: Disclosure protects users from hidden risks; a guarantee can turn into a real liability overnight.

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT a contingent liability?
options: Outstanding salary for March
Guarantee given for a third party's loan
Bills discounted but not yet matured
Claims against the company not acknowledged as debts
mcqs.explain: Outstanding salary is a definite present obligation — a liability. The others depend on uncertain future events.

mcqs.q: A provision is recognised when there is a present obligation from past events, a probable outflow, and:
options: A reliable estimate of the amount can be made
The amount is exactly known
The lawyer has filed a reply
The board has approved a dividend
mcqs.explain: The third condition is a reliable estimate; exact knowledge is not needed — that is why it is a provision and not a liability.

mcqs.q: If the possibility of an outflow on a claim is remote, the claim is:
options: Neither provided for nor disclosed
Provided for at the full amount
Disclosed as a contingent liability
Recognised as a liability
mcqs.explain: Disclosure of a contingent liability is not required when the possibility of outflow is remote.

mcqs.q: A penalty of ₹5,00,000 is under appeal. Management believes the appeal will probably fail. The company should:
options: Recognise a provision of ₹5,00,000
Disclose a contingent liability of ₹5,00,000
Show a contingent asset
Make no entry until the appeal is decided
mcqs.explain: Outflow is probable and the amount is known/estimable, so a provision is recognised.

mcqs.q: An item previously disclosed as a contingent liability becomes probable. A provision is recognised in:
options: The period in which the change in probability occurs
The period in which the claim was first made, by reopening it
The period in which payment is finally made
No period — it stays a contingent liability
mcqs.explain: The provision is recognised in the period when the probability changes.

mcqs.q: Claim filed by a company for ₹6,00,000 and an insurer's written admission of another claim of ₹2,50,000 (to be paid next month). The amount recognised as an asset is:
options: Nil
mcqs.explain: Only the admitted claim is virtually certain; the pending claim of ₹6,00,000 is a contingent asset and is not recognised.

mcqs.q: Disputed claims: (a) ₹3,00,000 — loss probable, estimate ₹2,40,000; (b) ₹1,80,000 — loss not probable; (c) ₹90,000 — remote. The amount to be disclosed as contingent liability is:
mcqs.explain: (a) is a provision (₹2,40,000 recognised); (c) is remote, so not disclosed; only (b) ₹1,80,000 is a contingent liability.

mcqs.q: Whether an item is a liability or only a contingent liability is usually decided by:

The amount involved
The age of the claim
The legal form of the creditor
mcqs.explain: Whether outflow is probable and measurable is a matter of management judgement.

mcqs.q: Provision for doubtful debts is an example of an amount retained to provide for:

A contingent asset
A capital receipt
A known liability of exact amount
mcqs.explain: A provision may be made for depreciation, renewal or diminution in value of assets — doubtful debts reduce the value of receivables.

questions.q: What is a contingent asset? How is it treated in the accounts, and when does it cease to be contingent?

model.text: A contingent asset is a possible asset, arising out of past events, whose existence will be settled only when certain uncertain future events, which the enterprise does not fully control, either take place or do not — for example, a claim being pursued in court.

Treatment: it is not recognised, because that could mean recognising income that may never be realised. It need not be disclosed in the financial statements; it is commonly mentioned in the approving authority's report (Board of Directors for a company) if an inflow of economic benefits is probable.

It is assessed continually. When the inflow becomes virtually certain, it is no longer a contingent asset — both the asset and the income it brings are booked in the period when that change takes place.

scheme.pt: Disclosure in Board's/approving authority's report if inflow probable
Recognised when virtually certain, in the period of change

remarks: Many answers wrongly say contingent assets are disclosed in notes like contingent liabilities.
mistakes: Treating "probable" as enough for recognition — the test is "virtually certain".
tips: Three short paragraphs: meaning, treatment, when it stops being contingent.

summary: Contingent asset: possible asset from past events, confirmed by uncertain future events. Not recognised; usually disclosed in the Board's report if inflow probable; recognised when virtually certain.

Contingent liability: possible obligation, or present obligation where outflow is not probable or not reliably measurable. Not recognised; disclosed in notes unless remote; becomes a provision when outflow turns probable.
Liability: present obligation, outflow on settlement — recognised.
Provision: present liability of uncertain amount, reliably estimable — recognised when present obligation + probable outflow + reliable estimate.
remember: Examples of contingent liabilities: unacknowledged claims, guarantees for third parties, bills discounted, disputed statutory dues.
Provide the best estimate, not the amount claimed.
Change of probability is dealt with in the period in which it occurs.
traps: Do not disclose contingent assets in notes the way contingent liabilities are disclosed.
Do not disclose remote contingent liabilities.
Do not add a recognised provision to the contingent liabilities note as well.

cases.title: Sunrise Hospitals Ltd — four uncertain matters
cases.case: At 31 March 2027 Sunrise Hospitals Ltd faces: (A) a negligence suit for ₹50,00,000 where its lawyers advise that a loss is probable and that ₹32,00,000 is the best estimate; (B) a municipal tax demand of ₹9,00,000 under appeal, which lawyers expect the hospital to win; (C) its own claim of ₹14,00,000 against an equipment supplier for a defective scanner — the supplier has not responded and the outcome is uncertain; and (D) a ₹1,00,000 claim by a visitor that lawyers say is frivolous with a remote chance of success.

mcqs.q: What amount should be recognised as a provision?
mcqs.explain: Only (A) meets all three tests — present obligation, probable outflow, reliable estimate. The best estimate, not the amount claimed, is provided.

mcqs.q: What total should be disclosed as contingent liabilities in the notes?
mcqs.explain: (B) is a contingent liability (outflow not probable). (D) is remote — not disclosed. (A) is a provision, not a contingent liability.

mcqs.q: How is the hospital's ₹14,00,000 claim against the supplier treated?
options: Not recognised; may be mentioned in the Board's report if inflow is probable
Recognised as income of ₹14,00,000
Shown as a receivable in the balance sheet
Netted off against the provision for (A)
mcqs.explain: It is a contingent asset — recognising it might record income that never arrives.

mcqs.q: In April 2027 the supplier admits the claim in writing and promises payment. What follows?
options: The asset and income are recognised in the period in which this change occurs
The 2026-27 accounts are reopened to show the income
It remains a contingent asset until cash is received
It is credited to capital reserve
mcqs.explain: When an inflow becomes virtually certain, the asset and related income are recognised in the period of the change.
